source_text: Paulus vero Apostolus de persecutore, qui primus Ecclesiae sanguinem fudit, postea gladium stylo mutans, et convertens machaeram in aratrum; lupus rapax Benjamin, dehinc ipse afferens escam secundum Jacob, qualiter martyria, jam et sibi optabilia, commendat! cum de Thessalonicensibus gaudens: Uti, inquit, gloriemur in vobis in Ecclesiis Dei pro tolerantia vestra et fide, in omnibus persecutionibus et pressuris, quibus sustinetis ostentamen justi judicii Dei, ut digni habeamini regno ejus, pro quo et patimini. Sicut et ad Romanos: Non solum autem, verum etiam exultantes in pressuris; certi quod pressura tolerantiam perficit, tolerantia vero probationem, probatio autem spem, spes vero non confundit. Et rursus: Quod si filii, et haeredes; haeredes quidem Dei, cohaeredes vero Christi: siquidem compatimur, uti et cum illo glorificemur. Reputo enim passiones hujus temporis non esse dignas ad gloriam, quae in nobis revelabitur. Et ideo postmodum: Quis, inquit, separabit nos a dilectione Christi? pressura, an angustia, an fames, an nuditas, an periculum, an machaera, secundum quod scriptum est: tui caussa mortificamur tota die, deputati sumus ut pecora jugulationis; sed in omnibus istis supervincimus pro eo qui nos dilexit. Persuasum enim habemus, quod neque mors, neque vita, neque virtus, neque sublimitas, neque profundum, neque alia conditio poterit nos a dilectione Dei separare, quae est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Sed et Corinthiis passiones suas enumerans, patiendum utique praefinivit: In laboribus abundantius, in carceribus plurimum, in mortibus saepius; a Judaeis quinquies quadragenas citra unam accepi, ter virgis caesus, semel lapidatus, et reliqua. Quae si magis incommoda quam martyria videbuntur, tamen rursus: Propter quod, inquit, boni duco in infirmitatibus, in injuriis, in necessitatibus, in persecutionibus, in angustiis pro Christo. Etiam in superioribus: Qui in omnibus tribulemur, sed non coangustemur; et indigeamus, sed non perindigeamus; quoniam persecutionibus agitemur, sed non derelinquamur; qui dejiciamur, sed non pereamus: semper mortificationem Christi Jesu in corpore nostro circumferentes. Sed etsi, inquit, exterior homo noster vitiatur, caro scilicet, vi persecutionum; sed interior renovatur die et die; anima scilicet spe promissionum. Nam quod ad praesens, temporale et leve pressurae nostrae per supergressum in supergressum aeternum pondus gloriae perficit nobis, non intuentibus quae videntur, sed quae non videntur. Quae enim videntur, temporalia, de incommodis dicens; quae vero non videntur, aeterna, de praemiis spondens. Thessalonicensibus vero de vinculis scribens, utique beatos affirmavit,, quibus donatum esset non tantum credere in Christum, sed etiam pro ipso pati: Eumdem, inquit, agonem habentes quem in me vidistis, et nunc audistis. Nam et si libor super sacrificium, gaudeo et congaudeo omnibus vobis, perinde et vos gaudete et congaudete mihi. Vides quam martyrii definiat felicitatem, cui de gaudio mutuo acquirit solemnitatem. Ut proximus denique voti sui factus est, qualiter de prospectu ejus exsultans Timotheo scribit? Ego enim jam libor, et tempus dijunctionis instat. Agonem bonum decertavi, cursum consummavi, fidem custodivi; superest corona, quam mihi Dominus illa die reddet, scilicet passionis. Satis et ipse supra allocutus: Fidelis sermo: si enim commortui sumus Christo, et convivemus; si sufferimus, et conregnabimus; si negaverimus, et ille nos negabit; si non credimus, ille fidelis est, negare se non potest. Ne ergo confundaris martyrio Domini nostri, neque me vinctum ejus; quia praedixerat: Non enim dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis et sanae mentis. Virtute enim patimur ex dilectione in Deum, et sana mente, cum ob innocentiam patimur. Sed et sicubi tolerantiam praecipit, quibus magis eam quam passionibus prospicit? sicubi ab idololatria divellit, quid ei magis quam martyria praevellit?
pass_a_gloss: Paul, indeed, an Apostle, concerning a persecutor, who first shed the Church's blood, afterwards changing the sword to a stylus, and converting the machete into a plow; a rapacious wolf of Benjamin, then himself bringing food, according to Jacob, in what way he commends martyrdoms, now already desirable to himself! When rejoicing about the Thessalonians: We glory, he says, in you in the Churches of God for your endurance and faith, in all the persecutions and pressures which you endure, a demonstration of the just judgment of God, so that you may be considered worthy of His kingdom, for which you also suffer. Just as also to the Romans: Not only, indeed, but also exulting in pressures; certain that pressure perfects endurance, endurance truly probation, probation indeed hope, hope indeed does not disappoint. And again: If we are sons, and heirs; heirs indeed of God, co-heirs truly of Christ: if we suffer, so that we may also be glorified with Him. I consider the passions of this time not to be worthy of the glory which will be revealed in us. And therefore afterwards: Who, he says, will separate us from the love of Christ? Pressure, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or sword, according to what is written: We are killed all day for Your sake, we are considered as sheep for slaughter; but in all these things we overcome on account of Him who loved us. For we are persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor virtue, nor height, nor depth, nor any other condition will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. But also to the Corinthians, enumerating his own passions, he certainly defined suffering: In labors more abundantly, in prisons more frequently, in deaths more often; from the Jews I received forty lashes minus one, three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, and the rest. If these seem more like hardships than martyrdoms, nevertheless again: On account of which, he says, I consider it good in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ. Also in the preceding: We are troubled in all things, but not constrained; and we are in need, but not in extreme need; since we are persecuted, but not abandoned; we are cast down, but not perishing: always carrying the mortification of Christ Jesus in our body. But if, he says, our outer man is being destroyed, namely the flesh, by the power of persecutions; but the inner man is being renewed day by day; namely the soul, by the hope of promises. For what is present, our temporary and light pressure, through the surpassing into the eternal weight of glory, perfects for us, not looking at what is seen, but what is not seen. For what is seen is temporary, speaking about hardships; what is not seen is eternal, promising about rewards. To the Thessalonians, indeed, writing about chains, he certainly affirmed the blessedness of those to whom it was given not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for Him: Having the same struggle which you saw in me, and now hear. For even if I am poured out as a sacrifice, I rejoice and congratulate all of you, and you rejoice and congratulate me in the same way. You see how he defines the happiness of martyrdom, acquiring solemnity from mutual joy. So that, having become next to his own wish, he writes to Timothy, exulting about his own prospect? For I am already being poured out, and the time of departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; there remains a crown, which the Lord will give me on that day, namely of passion. It is a faithful saying: if we have died with Christ, and live with Him; if we suffer, we will also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He will also deny us; if we do not believe, He is faithful, He cannot deny Himself. Therefore, do not be ashamed of the martyrdom of our Lord, nor of me being bound for Him; because He predicted: For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power, and love, and a sound mind. For we suffer with power from love for God, and with a sound mind, when we suffer for innocence. But also, wherever he commands endurance, for whom does he foresee it more than for martyrdoms? Wherever he tears away from idolatry, what does he tear away more than martyrdoms?

pass_b_english: Paul, once a persecutor who shed the Church's blood, later traded his sword for a pen and his machete for a plow, becoming a force for good, just like the rapacious wolf of Benjamin, who eventually brought food to the table, as Jacob had foretold. Now Paul commends martyrdom, which has become desirable to him, and he glories in the Thessalonians' endurance and faith in the face of persecution, seeing it as a testament to God's just judgment, which will ultimately make them worthy of His kingdom, for which they suffer (2 Timothy 4:7-8).

Paul's message to the Romans is similar: not only do they endure pressure, but they also find joy in it, because pressure refines their endurance, which in turn leads to spiritual maturity, and that maturity gives them hope, a hope that never disappoints. As children of God and co-heirs with Christ, they suffer so that they can be glorified with Him, and Paul believes that the struggles of this life are nothing compared to the glory that will be revealed in them. He asks, what could possibly separate them from Christ's love - hardship, distress, hunger, nakedness, danger, or sword? Nothing, he says, can separate them from God's love, which is in Christ Jesus their Lord (Romans 8:35-39).

Paul himself suffered greatly, and he tells the Corinthians about his experiences: he was in labor more often, in prison more frequently, and faced death more times than he can count; he was beaten, stoned, and faced all sorts of hardships. Yet, he considers it all good, because it happened for Christ's sake, and he knows that even in weakness, injury, and persecution, he can find joy. He and the Corinthians are troubled on every side, but they're not crushed; they're perplexed, but they're not abandoned; they're persecuted, but they're not forsaken; they're struck down, but they're not destroyed, all because they carry the death of Christ Jesus in their bodies, and that gives them life (2 Timothy 1:7).

Even when their bodies are being destroyed by persecution, Paul says, their inner selves are being renewed day by day, because they have the hope of eternal promises. What they're going through now is temporary and light, but it's preparing them for an eternal weight of glory, and that's what matters - not what they see, but what they don't see. The things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal, and that's where their reward lies. Paul writes to the Thessalonians about his chains, but he's not complaining; instead, he's affirming the blessedness of those who not only believe in Christ but also suffer for Him, just as he does. He's fighting the good fight, and he's finishing the course, and when it's all over, he'll receive a crown from the Lord, a crown of passion, and that's what makes all the suffering worth it.

Paul's message is clear: if they've died with Christ, they'll live with Him; if they suffer, they'll reign with Him; if they deny Him, He'll deny them; but if they don't believe, He's still faithful, because He cannot deny Himself. So, they shouldn't be ashamed of the Lord's martyrdom or of Paul being bound for Him, because God didn't give them a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and a sound mind. They suffer with power, love, and a sound mind, because they're innocent, and that's what makes their martyrdom worthwhile. Paul commands endurance, and he foresees it more for martyrdom than for anything else; he tears them away from idolatry, and what he's tearing away is martyrdom itself, because that's the ultimate test of their faith.

review.notes: Pass B contains several significant errors in translation and interpretation that violate the rules of fidelity and agency. 1. In the first paragraph of Pass B, it translates 'lupus rapax Benjamin' (the rapacious wolf of Benjamin) as 'becoming a force for good, just like the rapacious wolf of Benjamin', which misrepresents the Latin structure where the wolf is the subject/description of Paul himself, not a comparison to a force for good. 2. In the third paragraph of Pass B, it translates 'semper mortificationem Christi Jesu in corpore nostro circumferentes' as 'all because they carry the death of Christ Jesus in their bodies, and that gives them life'. The Latin 'mortificationem' (mortification/death-dealing/dying) and 'circumferentes' (carrying around/encompassing) are not rendered as 'gives them life'; Pass B adds a positive outcome ('gives them life') not present in the source text. 3. In the final paragraph of Pass B, it translates 'quid ei magis quam martyria praevellit?' (what does he [Paul] prevent/tear away from him [the believer] more than martyrdoms?) as 'what he's tearing away is martyrdom itself'. This is a logical reversal; the Latin asks what is being removed from the person *more* than martyrdom (implying martyrdom is the tool of removal from idolatry), whereas Pass B suggests martyrdom is the thing being removed. 4. Pass B adds 'they're perplexed' for 'indigeamus' (we are in need), which is a mistranslation of 'indigeamus' (to lack/be in need).
reasons: Pass B: 'becoming a force for good, just like the rapacious wolf of Benjamin' misrepresents 'lupus rapax Benjamin, dehinc ipse afferens escam' (the rapacious wolf of Benjamin, then himself bringing food); Pass B: 'and that gives them life' is an addition not found in 'semper mortificationem Christi Jesu in corpore nostro circumferentes'; Pass B: 'what he's tearing away is martyrdom itself' reverses the sense of 'quid ei magis quam martyria praevellit?'; Pass B: 'they're perplexed' is a mistranslation of 'indigeamus' (we are in need).

review.notes: Pass B misrepresents the Latin text by omitting key content and altering meaning. For example, 'Paul, once a persecutor who shed the Church's blood, later traded his sword for a pen and his machete for a plow' is not in the Latin. Also, 'Paul commends martyrdom, which has become desirable to him' is not supported by the Latin. The Latin says 'martyria, jam et sibi optabilia, commendat' which means 'martyrs, now also desirable to himself, commends' (not 'martyrdom, which has become desirable to him').
reasons: Pass B omits key content from the Latin, such as 'lupus rapax Benjamin, dehinc ipse afferens escam secundum Jacob, qualiter martyria, jam et sibi optabilia, commendat!' which is not reflected in the English translation.
Pass B misrepresents the Latin by stating 'Paul, once a persecutor who shed the Church's blood, later traded his sword for a pen and his machete for a plow' which is not in the Latin text.

Pass B incorrectly cites '2 Timothy 4:7-8' for 'I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith' which is not the correct citation for this passage in the Latin text.
